interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the output voltage move until the inductor's two shaded areas are equal, settling at D × 48 V, when you drag the duty cycle.
interactive.title: The balancing inductor
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
A short lesson in thirteen small screens. Most show one picture, the balancing inductor. A 48 V battery, chosen for the example, feeds a load that draws a steady 10 A, also chosen. A picker above chooses the circuit: Buck or Boost. The circuit is drawn small at the top. First comes the switch, a transistor with its gate. Then come the diode, the inductor, the capacitor and the load. The inductor is 100 µH, chosen. While the switch is on, it and its current path are drawn bold. While it is off, the diode and its path are bold. In Buck the switch runs from the battery to the inductor, and the diode from 0 V to the same point. In Boost the inductor runs from the battery to the switch. The switch goes to 0 V. The diode runs from that same point to the output. A duty cycle slider sets D from 10% to 90%, in steps of 5%. In Boost it stops at 75%. A frequency slider sets the switching frequency from 10 kHz to 100 kHz, in steps of 5 kHz. Each screen sets where they open.

Below the circuit, two plots share a time axis that shows three switching cycles, slowed down. The upper plot is the voltage across the inductor. While the switch is on it sits above the zero line, and while it is off it sits below. In each cycle the area above the line is shaded and labelled on. The area below is shaded and labelled off. In Buck the on height is Vin − Vout and the off depth is Vout. In Boost the on height is Vin and the off depth is Vout − Vin. Each area is its height times its time. The time is D × T on and (1 − D) × T off. T is one cycle, 1 ÷ f. At 50 kHz, T is 20 µs. The lower plot is the inductor's current. It ramps up while the voltage is above the line. It ramps down while the voltage is below. The coil's current changes at its voltage ÷ L amps a second, from v = L di/dt. A dashed line marks the inductor's average current. A Play button runs a cursor along the cycles, and a time slider drags it.

When D or the circuit changes, the output does not jump. It moves towards its new value over about two seconds of the slowed picture, a sketch of the settling. While it moves, the two areas differ. If the on area is bigger, the current ends each cycle a little higher than it began. The extra charges the capacitor, so the output rises. If the off area is bigger, the current drifts down, and the output falls. The output stops where the areas are equal. In Buck that is Vout = D × Vin: 24 V at 50%, 12 V at 25%. In Boost it is Vout = Vin ÷ (1 − D): 96 V at 50%, 192 V at 75%. A screen can stop the picture partway, with the output at a stated voltage.

Up to three readouts sit under the plots. They wrap onto two lines on a narrow phone. Ripple and its band appear from screen 8 on. Screens 6 and 10 leave out the battery current. Output voltage is Vout. Ripple is the current's rise in each cycle as a share of the inductor's average current. The rise is the on height × D ÷ (f × L). In Buck the average current is the load's 10 A. So 48 V to 24 V at 50 kHz rises 24 V × 10 µs ÷ 100 µH = 2.4 A. That is 24%. In Boost the average current is 10 A ÷ (1 − D), 20 A at 50%. The rise is 48 V × 10 µs ÷ 100 µH = 4.8 A, also 24%. In Buck a band beside the ripple readout marks 20% to 40%, the usual choice for a buck's ripple. Battery current is the average current from the battery. It is the load's power, Vout × 10 A, over 48 V. That is 5 A at 50% in Buck, and 20 A at 50% in Boost.

The screens.

1, a puzzle: the picture shows the Buck circuit at rest, D at 50%, with the plots and readouts hidden. “You need 24 V at 10 A from a 48 V battery. A transistor held part on drops the other 24 V. How much heat does it make?” Offered: “About 240 W”; “Next to nothing, as it is a transistor”; “About 480 W”. Hint for next to nothing: “Part on, it has 24 V across it and 10 A through it.” Hint for 480 W: “Only half the battery's voltage is across the transistor.” Why: “About 240 W, as much as the load gets. Part on, the transistor has 24 V across it and 10 A through it. A switch kept fully on or fully off wastes little heat.[^1] So chop the battery instead, and smooth what comes out.” A right Check shows the plots and the readouts.

2, show: Chop it. Buck, D at 50%, Play running. The words: “A buck converter is a switching transistor followed by a diode, an inductor and a capacitor.[^2] Here a 48 V battery feeds a load that draws 10 A. While the switch is on, current flows from the battery through the inductor to the load. When the switch opens, the inductor keeps its current going through the diode.[^3] That is the freewheeling diode again. The share of each cycle the switch is on is the duty cycle, D. Play it at D = 50%.” Read: with D at 50%, the switch carries the current for the first half of each cycle. The diode carries it for the second half. The inductor's current keeps flowing all through the cycle. Still: Buck, D 50%, 50 kHz, settled, cursor three quarters of the way through a cycle.

3, a puzzle: Buck, D at 50%, settled at 24 V, the cursor in an on-time. “The switch is on. The battery is 48 V and the output 24 V. What voltage is across the inductor?” Offered: “24 V, the difference”; “48 V, the whole battery”; “0 V, as current flows freely”. Hint for 48 V: “The inductor's far end sits at the output, not at 0 V.” Hint for 0 V: “Its current is climbing. A coil's current changes only with a voltage across it.” Why: “24 V. One end sees the battery's 48 V through the switch. The other end sits at the output's 24 V. That 24 V across it makes its current climb steadily, as v = L di/dt says.” A right Check lights the on part of the voltage plot, 24 V above the line.

4, show: Two areas. Buck, D at 50%, settled at 24 V. The words: “The upper plot is the inductor's voltage. While the switch is on, it is the battery less the output, and the current climbs. While it is off, the diode holds the inductor's input end near 0 V. The inductor now sees the output the other way round, and the current falls. Each shaded area is a voltage times a time. Divide it by L to get how far the current climbs or falls. The current ends each cycle where it began. So the two areas must be equal. Its average voltage is zero.[^4]” Read: with D at 50%, the output sits at 24 V. The area above the line is 24 V for half the cycle. It equals the area below, 24 V for the other half. The current ramps up and back down to where it started. Still: Buck, D 50%, 50 kHz, settled, cursor 360°.

5, a puzzle: Buck, D at 50%, the picture stopped with the output at 20 V on its way up. “The output has reached only 20 V, with D at 50%. What happens next?” Offered: “The area above is bigger, so the current climbs and the output rises”; “The area below is bigger, so the output falls”; “Nothing, as the areas already balance”. Hint for falls: “Above the line: 48 − 20 = 28 V for half the cycle. Below: 20 V for half. Which is bigger?” Hint for balance: “Compare 28 V and 20 V, each for half the cycle.” Why: “The area above is bigger, 28 V against 20 V, each for half the cycle. So the current climbs a little more each cycle than it falls. The extra current charges the capacitor, and the output rises. That shrinks the area above and grows the one below. It stops at 24 V, where they balance.” A right Check lets the picture run on. The output settles at 24 V.

6, show: The rule. Buck, D from 50% to 25%, the battery current hidden. The words: “Equal areas give the rule. The area above is (Vin − Vout) × D × T, where T is one cycle. The area below is Vout × (1 − D) × T.[^5] Set them equal, and T cancels. Multiply out, and the Vout × D on each side cancels too. That leaves Vout = D × Vin. So 50% of 48 V gives 24 V, and 25% gives 12 V. Drag D, and the output moves until the areas match again.” Read: with D at 25%, the output has settled at 12 V. The area above is 36 V for a quarter of the cycle. It matches the area below, 12 V for three quarters. Still: Buck, D 25%, 50 kHz, settled, cursor 360°.

7, a puzzle: Buck, D at 25%, the output at 12 V, the battery current hidden. “The load still draws 10 A. What average current does the 48 V battery supply?” Offered: “About 2.5 A”; “About 10 A, the same as the load”; “About 40 A”. Hint for 10 A: “That is what a series resistor would take. When does the battery give current here?” Hint for 40 A: “A buck lowers the voltage. Does the battery need more current than the load, or less?” Why: “About 2.5 A. The battery gives current only while the switch is on, 10 A for a quarter of each cycle. That averages 2.5 A, or 120 W from 48 V. The load gets 12 V × 10 A, also 120 W. A series resistor would take the full 10 A and burn 360 W.” A right Check shows the battery current, 2.5 A.

8, show: Ripple. Buck, D at 50%, the frequency from 50 kHz to 100 kHz. The words: “The lower plot is the inductor's current. It ramps up and down around the load's 10 A. Each cycle it climbs (Vin − Vout) × D ÷ (f × L). Here 24 V across 100 µH for 10 µs gives 2.4 A, 24% of 10 A. The ripple is usually chosen to be 20% to 40% of the output current.[^6] The capacitor takes the ripple, so the load sees near-steady DC. Raise the frequency, and the ripple shrinks. But every switch-over wastes a little heat, so the switch runs hotter.” Read: at 100 kHz the current climbs 1.2 A and falls 1.2 A each cycle. The ripple reads 12%. The output stays at 24 V. Still: Buck, D 50%, 100 kHz, settled, cursor 360°.

9, a puzzle: Buck, D at 50%, 50 kHz, the ripple reading 24%. “The switching frequency drops to 25 kHz. What is the ripple now?” Offered: “4.8 A, 48% of the load”; “1.2 A, 12% of the load”; “2.4 A, as the frequency does not matter”. Hint for 1.2 A: “At a lower frequency each on-time is longer. Does the current climb further, or less far?” Hint for 2.4 A: “The on-time is now 20 µs, not 10 µs.” Why: “4.8 A. At 25 kHz each cycle lasts 40 µs, so the switch is on for 20 µs. 24 V across 100 µH for twice as long climbs twice as far. That is 48% of 10 A, above the 20% to 40% guide. A bigger inductor brings it back. So does a higher frequency, at the cost of more switching heat.” A right Check sets 25 kHz. The ripple reads 48%, and the output stays at 24 V.

10, show: Boost. Boost, D at 50%, the battery current hidden. The words: “The picker now shows Boost. The same parts are rearranged. The inductor comes straight off the battery. The switch shorts its far end to 0 V. While on, the inductor sees the whole 48 V and stores energy.[^7] When off, it drives its current through the diode into an output above the battery.[^8] The areas still balance: Vin × D = (Vout − Vin) × (1 − D). The Vin × D terms cancel, leaving Vin = Vout × (1 − D). So Vout = Vin ÷ (1 − D), 96 V at 50%.” Read: in Boost at 50%, the area above is 48 V for half the cycle. It matches the area below, 48 V for the other half. The output reads 96 V. Still: Boost, D 50%, 50 kHz, settled, cursor 360°.

11, a puzzle: Boost, D at 50%, the output at 96 V, the battery current hidden. “This boost gives 96 V to a load drawing 10 A. What average current does the 48 V battery supply?” Offered: “About 20 A”; “About 10 A, the same as the load”; “About 5 A, as in the buck”. Hint for 10 A: “Compare the power: 96 V × 10 A out, but 48 V × 10 A in.” Hint for 5 A: “A boost raises the voltage. Where must the extra power come from?” Why: “About 20 A. The load takes 96 V × 10 A = 960 W. With little lost, the battery must supply that too. 960 W ÷ 48 V = 20 A. A boost trades current for voltage. It does not make energy.” A right Check shows the battery current, 20 A.

12, a mixed puzzle: Boost, D at 50%, the output at 96 V. “The boost must give 192 V from the 48 V battery. What duty cycle?” Offered: “75%”; “25%”; “None, as no chopper gives four times its input”. Hint for 25%: “That is the buck way round. In a boost, 1 − D = Vin ÷ Vout.” Hint for none: “In the ideal rule, Vout = Vin ÷ (1 − D). What 1 − D gives four times?” Why: “75%. Four times the battery needs 1 − D = ¼, so D = 0.75. Check the areas at 50 kHz. Above the line is 48 V × 15 µs. Below is 144 V × 5 µs. Both come to 720 V·µs. The battery current is now 40 A for the load's 10 A.” A right Check sets D to 75%. The output settles at 192 V, and the battery current reads 40 A.

13, a mixed puzzle: Buck, D at 50%, the output at 24 V. The picture keeps its 48 V battery. The question is about a battery that has run down. “The battery runs down from 48 V to 40 V. The buck must still give 24 V. What duty cycle holds it?” Offered: “60%”; “50%, unchanged”; “40%”. Hint for 50%: “50% of 40 V is only 20 V.” Hint for 40%: “A smaller battery needs a bigger share of it, not a smaller one.” Why: “60%. D = Vout ÷ Vin = 24 ÷ 40 = 0.6. A controller can do this as it runs. It moves D to hold the output as the battery voltage changes. On a ship's DC network, power sources can join the DC bus through converters like these.[^9]” A right Check keeps the picture as it is.

Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers, stacked. Each can wrap onto more lines on a narrow phone. A wrong pick gets its one-line hint. Why? explains the answer. Continue moves on. The finish words sum up the lesson and end: “Make D follow a sine in a bridge of switches, and the output's average follows that sine. That is how an inverter builds AC.”
interactive.ignores: The switch and diode are drawn ideal. A real switch and diode each drop a little voltage and waste a little power. So a real buck needs a slightly larger D. The inductor is drawn with no resistance. The capacitor is drawn big enough that the output's own ripple is too small to see. The load draws a steady 10 A at any voltage. A real load's current would change with its voltage. The inductor's current never falls to zero here. At a very light load it can, and then the rules change. The settling is a sketch. A real output can overshoot before it settles. A controller manages that. Time is slowed down. At 50 kHz one cycle lasts 20 µs.

explain.text:
Switch a battery on and off fast, and smooth the pulses with an inductor and a capacitor. You get a steady lower DC. It is the battery voltage times the share of time the switch is on. Rearrange the same parts, and you get a steady higher DC instead.

A [[buck converter]] is a switching transistor followed by a diode, an inductor and a capacitor. The share of each cycle the switch is on is the [[duty cycle]], D. While the switch is on, the inductor has the battery at one end and the output at the other. So it sees Vin − Vout, and its current climbs, as v = L di/dt says. When the switch opens, the inductor keeps its current going through the diode. The diode holds that end near 0 V. So the inductor now sees Vout the other way round, and its current falls.

Draw the voltage across the inductor against time. Each area is a voltage times a time. Divided by L, it is how far the current climbs or falls, as v = L di/dt says. In steady running the current must end each cycle where it began. So the area above the line must equal the area below. The voltage across the inductor averages zero.[^4] That gives (Vin − Vout) × D = Vout × (1 − D). Multiply out, and Vout × D cancels from both sides. That leaves Vout = D × Vin. So 48 V at 50% gives 24 V, and at 25% gives 12 V. If the output is too low, the area above is bigger. So the current gains a little each cycle. That extra current charges the capacitor until the areas balance. The switch is fully on or fully off, so it wastes little heat. The battery gives current only while the switch is on. At 50% that is 5 A on average for a 10 A load. So power in matches power out, less small losses. That is why switching supplies are more efficient than a transistor held part on. The current ripples by (Vin − Vout) × D ÷ (f × L) each cycle. That ripple is usually chosen to be 20% to 40% of the output current.[^6]

A [[boost converter]] puts the inductor straight off the battery. Its switch runs from the inductor's far end to 0 V. While on, the inductor sees the whole of Vin and stores energy. When off, it drives its current through the diode into an output above the battery. The same balance holds: Vin × D = (Vout − Vin) × (1 − D). That gives Vout = Vin ÷ (1 − D). So 48 V at 50% gives 96 V. The battery then supplies more current than the load takes, 20 A for 10 A. A converter does not make energy. Make D follow a sine, and the output's average follows a sine too. That is how a drive builds AC. This is a simplified picture. The switch and diode are ideal, and the inductor current never falls to zero. **Chop DC through an inductor and a capacitor, and the inductor's zero average voltage sets the output: D × Vin for a buck, Vin ÷ (1 − D) for a boost.**

analogy.text: A buck works like a moving-coil meter on chopped DC. Feed it 48 V pulses, on half the time, and it reads about 24 V. Its needle is too heavy to follow each pulse. So it settles where its spring balances the average push. Change the share of on-time, and the needle moves to a new average, D × 48 V.
analogy.breaks: A meter only shows the average. A buck's inductor carries the load's whole current and passes on the battery's energy. So the load gets the average as real power. And a meter can never read above its pulses. A boost's output sits above its battery.

practice.text:
Isolate and prove dead on both sides before you work on a converter. Its capacitors can hold charge, as a DC link does. A boost's output also sits above its battery.

- Find the input voltage, the output you need and the load current.
- Buck: D = Vout ÷ Vin. Boost: D = 1 − Vin ÷ Vout.
- Battery current, near enough: a buck's is D × the load current. A boost's is the load current ÷ (1 − D).
- Buck ripple: (Vin − Vout) × D ÷ (f × L). Compare it with 20% to 40% of the output current.[^6]

**Rules of thumb:** a higher frequency or a bigger inductor gives less ripple. The frequency sets the ripple, not the output voltage. As the battery voltage changes, D must change to hold the output.

**Worked example:** a 48 V battery must feed a 12 V load drawing 10 A, switching at 50 kHz through 100 µH. D = 12 ÷ 48 = 0.25, so 25%. The battery supplies about 0.25 × 10 = 2.5 A, or 120 W. That matches the load's 12 V × 10 A. The ripple is 36 × 0.25 ÷ (50,000 × 0.0001) = 1.8 A, 18% of 10 A. That is a little under the 20% to 40% guide. So this inductor is on the large side. If the battery runs down to 40 V, D must rise to 12 ÷ 40 = 30%.

**Common mistakes**
- Thinking a buck burns off the difference like a resistor. A resistor dropping 48 V to 12 V for 10 A burns 360 W.
- Expecting a boost to make energy. Its battery current is more than its load current.
- Using the buck rule on a boost. At 50%, a buck gives 24 V from 48 V, and a boost gives 96 V.
- Thinking the frequency sets the voltage. It sets the ripple.
- Reading D as on-time over off-time. It is on-time over the whole cycle.
